$comment: Teaching content for cl_api_core. Knowledge points are ordered: the first covers the most basic idea, later ones the harder cases. reviewQuestions are held back from the lesson so a spaced review is not a re-run.

knowledgePoints.name: Three arguments, one call
knowledgePoints.teach:
Everything in this section is one function with three required arguments.

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5",     # which Claude
    max_tokens=1024,              # ceiling on the output
    messages=[                    # the conversation so far
        {"role": "user", "content": "Summarise this survey report."}
    ],
)

messages is an array of {role, content} objects, not a string. That shape is what makes multi-turn conversation possible later, and it is why the API can be stateless.

model, max_tokens, messages. Leave any one out and the request is rejected.

Everything else — system, temperature, tools, stream — is optional and gets added to this same call.

questions.q: Which set of arguments must every messages.create call carry?
options: model, system, messages
model, max_tokens, messages
model, temperature, messages
api_key, model, messages
questions.explain: model, max_tokens, messages. The system prompt and temperature are optional, and the key is supplied to the client, not to the call.

questions.q: What is the `messages` argument, structurally?
options: A string containing the user's question
An array of objects, each with a role and content
A dictionary mapping usernames to their questions
A single object with a `user` and an `assistant` key
questions.explain: An array of {role, content} objects. That the conversation is a list is the fact everything about multi-turn state depends on.

knowledgePoints.name: Where the key lives
knowledgePoints.teach:
The client is authorised by an API key, and the key belongs in an environment file — .env.local — that is excluded from version control.

The reason is not tidiness. A key hardcoded in a source file is a key that gets committed, pushed, and scraped off GitHub by automated crawlers within minutes of becoming public. Rotating a leaked key is the easy part; the charges billed before you notice are not.

The same logic rules out shipping the key to a mobile app or a browser: anything running on a device you do not control can be read. Calls from a client app go through your server, which holds the key.

questions.q: Why is an API key kept in .env.local rather than in the file that calls the API?
options: Environment variables are read faster than string literals
So it is not committed to version control and scraped once the repo is public
The SDK cannot read a key passed as an argument
It lets you use a different key per model tier
questions.explain: A hardcoded key gets committed and pushed. Public-repo crawlers find keys in minutes.

questions.q: Your mobile app needs Claude-generated summaries. Where does the API key go?
options: Bundled with the app, obfuscated so it cannot be extracted
In the app's environment configuration at build time
On your own server, which the app calls and which calls Anthropic
In the user's device keychain, entered on first launch
questions.explain: Anything shipped to a device you do not control can be extracted, obfuscated or not. The key stays on your server.

reviewQuestions.q: A request fails validation before it reaches the model. Which omission would do that?
options: No system prompt
No max_tokens
No temperature
No stop_sequences
reviewQuestions.explain: max_tokens is one of the three required arguments. The other three named here are all optional.

knowledgePoints.name: content is a list, not a string
knowledgePoints.teach:
The most common first bug in a Claude integration:

print(response.content[0].text)   # works today

response.content is an array of typed blocks. Each block has a type, and a single response can carry several of them at once:

typewhat it holds
textprose for the user
tool_usea tool Claude wants run, with its input
thinkingreasoning, when extended thinking is on
server_tool_usea tool Anthropic ran server-side

The moment you enable tools or thinking, content[0] stops reliably being the text — and the failure is silent, because index 0 still exists and still has a value.

for block in response.content:
    if block.type == "text":     handle_text(block.text)
    elif block.type == "tool_use": run_tool(block)

questions.q: Why is `response.content[0].text` described as a latent bug rather than an error?
options: It raises an exception on every response that contains a tool call
It works until a response leads with a non-text block, and then it silently reads the wrong thing
It only fails when streaming is enabled
It works but is slower than iterating
questions.explain: Latent is the right word: index 0 keeps existing. It just stops being the block you meant once thinking or tool_use blocks appear.

questions.q: What is the safe general shape for reading a response?
options: Concatenate every block's text field
Loop over content and dispatch on each block's type
Read content[-1], since the final block is always the answer
Call response.text(), which flattens the blocks
questions.explain: Loop and switch on block.type. Blocks are typed precisely so that different kinds get different handling.

reviewQuestions.q: You turn on extended thinking and your UI starts printing reasoning where the answer should be. What happened?
options: Thinking replaces the text block rather than joining it
The code reads content[0], which is now a thinking block rather than a text block
Thinking output is returned in a separate field the UI is not reading
max_tokens is being consumed by reasoning before the answer starts
reviewQuestions.explain: A new block type appeared ahead of the text. Code indexing content[0] follows it straight into the wrong block.

reviewQuestions.q: Which is true of a single Claude response?
options: It contains exactly one content block
It can contain several blocks of different types
It contains one block per tool defined in the request
Block count equals the number of turns in the conversation
reviewQuestions.explain: One response, several blocks — text and tool_use together is the normal case once tools are in play.

knowledgePoints.name: Four values, four different actions
knowledgePoints.teach:
stop_reason is the field that says why generation stopped. It is small, and everything agentic branches on it.

valuemeaningwhat your code does
end_turnClaude finishedUse the answer
tool_useClaude wants a tool runRun it, send the result back, go again
max_tokensHit your ceiling mid-sentenceRaise the budget or shorten the task — not a prompt bug
stop_sequenceHit a string you suppliedExpected, if you set one

A truncated answer and a finished answer look identical in the text. Only stop_reason distinguishes them.

This is why you never diagnose a cut-off response by re-reading the prompt first. Check the field that already told you.

questions.q: A generated draft ends mid-sentence. Which stop_reason distinguishes a budget problem from a prompt problem, and what value indicates the budget?
options: stop_reason == end_turn means the budget ran out
stop_reason == max_tokens means it hit the ceiling you set
stop_reason == stop_sequence means the model gave up
stop_reason is absent when a response is truncated
questions.explain: max_tokens is a ceiling, and hitting it is reported plainly. The prompt was fine; the budget was not.

questions.q: Which stop_reason means your code has more work to do before the turn is over?
options: end_turn
tool_use
stop_sequence
max_tokens
questions.explain: tool_use: Claude is waiting on a result from you. It is the continue condition of every agent loop.

reviewQuestions.q: What is the exit condition of an agent loop?
options: The tools array is empty
stop_reason is end_turn
The response contains a text block
max_tokens is reached
reviewQuestions.explain: end_turn. A text block can appear alongside a tool_use block, so its presence proves nothing about being finished.

reviewQuestions.q: Your summariser has produced clean output for months, then starts truncating on long inputs. What do you check first?
options: Whether the system prompt has drifted
stop_reason, to see whether it is max_tokens
Whether temperature is too high
The model tier, in case it was downgraded
reviewQuestions.explain: The response already carries the diagnosis. max_tokens means the ceiling is now too low for the inputs you are getting.

knowledgePoints.name: Stable instructions have their own home
knowledgePoints.teach:
The system parameter sits beside messages, not inside it:

client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    system="You are a terse senior code reviewer. Lead with the most serious issue.",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": diff}],
)

What belongs there: role, domain, and behaviour that hold across every request. What does not: the thing you want done this time.

The split is not cosmetic. Because the system prompt is stable, it is:

  • the same bytes on every call — which is exactly what prompt caching requires,
  • processed before the messages, so it frames everything after it,
  • separable from user-supplied content, which matters when that content is untrusted.

Omit it entirely when there is no standing instruction. An empty system prompt is better than a vague one.

questions.q: Which instruction belongs in the system parameter?
options: “Summarise the report below in three bullets.”
“You are a terse senior code reviewer.”
“Here is the customer's latest message.”
“Return valid JSON for this one request.”
questions.explain: Role and standing behaviour go in system. The other three are about this particular request and belong in the user turn.

questions.q: What property of the system prompt makes it the best candidate for caching?
options: It is processed last, so the cache is written after the response
It rarely changes, so the same bytes are re-sent on every call
It is exempt from the 1,024-token minimum
It is the only part of a request that can be cached
questions.explain: Stability is the whole criterion. A cache hit requires a byte-identical prefix, and stable content is what stays identical.

reviewQuestions.q: Every request your service makes should be answered in the same clinical, non-speculative register. Where does that instruction go?
options: Prepended to each user message
In the system parameter
In an assistant prefill
In a stop sequence
reviewQuestions.explain: It holds across every request, so it is standing behaviour — and putting it in system also keeps it cacheable.

knowledgePoints.name: The API remembers nothing
knowledgePoints.teach:
A chatbot that answers every question as though it were the first is not broken. It is working exactly as a stateless API works.

Claude has no memory between calls. The only thing it knows is what is in the messages array you just sent.

Multi-turn conversation exists because you build it, appending both halves of every exchange:

messages = []

messages.append({"role": "user", "content": question})
response = client.messages.create(model=M, max_tokens=1024, messages=messages)

# both halves — the assistant turn goes back in too
messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})

messages.append({"role": "user", "content": follow_up})   # now Claude can see the first exchange

Note what is appended for the assistant turn: response.content, the complete block array — not the string you extracted for display. Dropping the non-text blocks here is what breaks tool loops later.

questions.q: Your chatbot cannot remember what the user said two messages ago. What is missing?
options: A session id on the request
Your code is not appending previous turns to the messages array
conversation_memory is not enabled on the account
The system prompt does not instruct Claude to remember
questions.explain: The API is stateless. History exists only because you resend it, every time.

questions.q: What do you append for the assistant's half of a turn?
options: The extracted text string you showed the user
The complete response.content block array
A summary of what Claude said, to save tokens
Nothing — only user turns are appended
questions.explain: The whole content array. Keeping only the visible text discards tool_use blocks and breaks the next turn.

reviewQuestions.q: Which statement about the Messages API is true?
options: It stores conversation history for 30 days
It is stateless; conversation history is whatever you resend
It stores history only when a system prompt is set
It keeps history per API key automatically
reviewQuestions.explain: Stateless. Every call is complete on its own, which is also why context cost grows with conversation length.

reviewQuestions.q: What is the cost consequence of maintaining conversation history yourself?
options: None — history is billed once when it is first sent
The whole history is re-sent and re-billed as input on every turn
History is billed at the output rate
Only the most recent turn is billed
reviewQuestions.explain: Everything you resend is input tokens again. It is why compaction and caching exist.

knowledgePoints.name: max_tokens is a ceiling, not a target
knowledgePoints.teach:
max_tokens sets the maximum length of the output. Two things people expect of it that are not true:

  • It is not a request for that much text. Setting 4096 does not make Claude write 4096 tokens.
  • It is not a soft limit. Hit it and generation stops mid-sentence, with stop_reason: "max_tokens".

So it is a safety valve — protection against a runaway generation billing you for output you never wanted — and the price of setting it too low is truncation, not brevity.

questions.q: You set max_tokens=4096 and get a 200-token answer. What happened?
options: The request failed silently and returned a partial response
Nothing unusual — max_tokens is a ceiling, and Claude finished early
The model tier caps output below your setting
temperature was too low to produce a longer answer
questions.explain: A ceiling, not a target. Claude writes what the task needs and stops with end_turn.

questions.q: What happens when generation reaches max_tokens?
options: Claude wraps up with a concluding sentence
Output stops wherever it is, with stop_reason max_tokens
The request is retried automatically with a higher limit
An error is returned and no content comes back
questions.explain: It stops dead, mid-sentence if that is where it lands, and reports max_tokens as the reason.

knowledgePoints.name: Temperature buys variation, not correctness
knowledgePoints.teach:
temperature runs 0 to 1 and changes how randomly the next token is sampled.

rangefits
lowfactual extraction, coding, deterministic transformations
mediumexplanation, constrained creativity
highbrainstorming, creative variation

Temperature does not guarantee a different answer, and it never guarantees a correct one.

Two failure modes follow from that. Turning temperature down does not make a wrong extraction right — it makes it consistently wrong, which is easier to notice but no more accurate. And turning it up to get variety on a factual task widens the distribution of things that are false.

questions.q: An extraction pipeline returns slightly different field values run to run. Which setting most directly addresses that?
options: Raise max_tokens
Lower temperature
Enable streaming
Add a stop sequence
questions.explain: Low temperature is the setting for deterministic transformations. It reduces variation — though it does not make the extraction correct.

questions.q: What does temperature 0 guarantee?
options: The same answer every time
A correct answer
Less randomness in sampling — but neither identical output nor correctness is promised
That Claude will refuse creative tasks
questions.explain: It reduces randomness. The course is explicit that it guarantees neither a different answer nor a right one.

reviewQuestions.q: Which of these is a budget rather than a quality setting?
options: temperature
max_tokens
system
model
reviewQuestions.explain: max_tokens caps spend and length. It says nothing about how good the output is.

knowledgePoints.name: Four rungs on one ladder
knowledgePoints.teach:
Capability and cost rise together, so the tiers are one ordered ladder:

tierpositionnatural work
Fablemost capable, above Opus, highest costwork where the extra capability is worth paying for
Opusdeep reasoningcomplex analysis, multi-step coding
Sonnetbalancedthe sweet spot for most production work
Haikufastest, cheapesthigh-volume, low-complexity: classification, extraction, routing

The three words to attach to Haiku are the ones that come up most on the exam: classification, extraction, routing. Those are its jobs, and they are jobs a large model does no better while costing far more.

questions.q: Ten thousand support tickets a day need sorting into five categories. Which tier?
options: Fable
Opus
Sonnet
Haiku
questions.explain: High volume, low complexity, and classification by name — Haiku's exact brief.

questions.q: Which tier sits above Opus in capability and cost?
options: Sonnet
Haiku
Fable
Nothing — Opus is the top tier
questions.explain: Fable is the most capable tier, above Opus, at the highest cost.

reviewQuestions.q: Which tier is described as the sweet spot for most production work?
options: Haiku
Sonnet
Opus
Fable
reviewQuestions.explain: Sonnet is the balanced default. Haiku is below it, Opus and Fable above.

reviewQuestions.q: A one-off multi-step regulatory trade-off analysis. Which tier is the natural fit?
options: Haiku
Sonnet
Opus
Whichever is cheapest — the task is one-off
reviewQuestions.explain: Deep reasoning and complex analysis is Opus's brief, and being one-off is exactly when its cost is affordable.

knowledgePoints.name: Search upward from the cheapest
knowledgePoints.teach:
The course's method is a search, and the direction matters.

  1. Build a small eval first — 20 to 30 representative examples.
  2. Run them through Haiku.
  3. If quality holds, stop. You are done.
  4. If it does not, step up to Sonnet.
  5. Reach for Opus only when the task genuinely needs it.

The right model is the cheapest one whose output you would actually ship.

Starting at the top and working down almost never happens in practice: once something works, nobody goes back to test whether something cheaper also would. So the direction of the search is the whole discipline.

response.usage reports input and output token counts — the numbers your bill is computed from, and the ones that make the difference between tiers concrete rather than theoretical.

questions.q: In what order do you test model tiers for a new feature?
options: Opus first for a quality ceiling, then down until quality breaks
Haiku first, stepping up only when quality does not hold
Sonnet first, then out to Haiku and Opus in parallel
Whichever tier the previous feature used
questions.explain: Cheapest first, stopping as soon as quality holds. Searching downward from the top rarely gets finished.

questions.q: What has to exist before the model comparison is meaningful?
options: A production traffic sample of at least 1,000 requests
An eval of 20–30 representative examples to score each model against
A fine-tuned baseline
A cost ceiling agreed with finance
questions.explain: 20–30 representative examples. Without a shared scoreboard, 'quality holds' is just an opinion.

knowledgePoints.name: One pipeline, several tiers
knowledgePoints.teach:
Model choice is per task, not per application. A single endpoint routinely spans tiers:

classify(ticket)      → Haiku    # cheap, high volume, easy
draft_reply(ticket)   → Sonnet   # the bulk of the work
rfp_response(ticket)  → Opus     # rare, high stakes, escalate

This is the same idea as the routing workflow pattern, seen from the cost side: classify with the cheap model, and let the classification decide which model handles the rest. The expensive tier only ever sees the fraction of traffic that needs it.

questions.q: A support pipeline classifies tickets, drafts most replies, and occasionally writes a full RFP response. What is the sensible model arrangement?
options: One tier for the whole pipeline, chosen for the hardest task
Different tiers per task — Haiku to classify, Sonnet to draft, Opus for the rare hard case
One tier for the whole pipeline, chosen for the most common task
Alternate tiers by request to spread cost
questions.explain: Route per task type. Sizing everything for the hardest case pays Opus prices on classification.

questions.q: Which field tells you what a request actually cost you?
options: response.stop_reason
response.usage
response.content
response.model
questions.explain: usage reports input and output token counts, which is what the bill is computed from.

reviewQuestions.q: How does the course define the right model for a task?
options: The most capable one your budget allows
The cheapest one whose output you would actually ship
Sonnet, unless benchmarks say otherwise
Whichever has the lowest latency at acceptable quality
reviewQuestions.explain: Cheapest shippable. It makes the decision an evidence question rather than a preference.

knowledgePoints.name: The lifecycle, in order
knowledgePoints.teach:
Streaming delivers the same response as a sequence of events rather than one payload:

message_start
  content_block_start
  content_block_delta   ← repeated, the actual text arriving
  content_block_stop
message_delta
message_stop

Notice the shape: the inner three events are per block. Streaming is the block structure you already know, unrolled in time — which is why a response with two blocks produces two content_block_start events.

Python offers three levels of convenience over the same lifecycle: client.messages.stream for the events, stream.text_stream for just the text deltas, and get_final_message() for the assembled result once it settles.

questions.q: Which event carries the text as it is generated?
options: message_start
content_block_start
content_block_delta
message_delta
questions.explain: content_block_delta, repeated. The start and stop events bracket each block.

questions.q: A streamed response contains a thinking block and a text block. How many content_block_start events do you see?
options: One
Two
One per delta
None — content_block_start only fires for text
questions.explain: The block lifecycle repeats per block. Two blocks, two starts.

knowledgePoints.name: What streaming does not fix
knowledgePoints.teach:
Streaming improves time-to-first-token and therefore the experience of waiting. That is the entire benefit.

Same model, same quality, same total latency to completion, same errors — and the same obligation to handle incomplete output.

In fact incomplete output gets more visible: a response truncated at max_tokens is streamed to the user word by word right up to the point it stops. The user watches it break. So streaming raises the stakes on checking stop_reason rather than lowering them.

questions.q: What does enabling streaming change?
options: Total latency to a complete answer
Time to first token, and nothing about output quality
The cost per token
The likelihood of hitting max_tokens
questions.explain: It is a perceived-latency fix. The response is the same response, arriving in pieces.

questions.q: Why does streaming make stop_reason handling more important, not less?
options: Streamed responses hit max_tokens more often
The user watches a truncated answer break off in real time
stop_reason is only available when streaming
Streaming disables server-side validation
questions.explain: The failure is now visible as it happens. Nothing about truncation changed — only who sees it.

reviewQuestions.q: Users complain about thirty seconds of blank screen on long generations. What do you turn on, and what does it not fix?
options: Streaming — it does not reduce total generation time
Streaming — it also reduces total generation time
A lower temperature — it does not improve quality
Compaction — it does not reduce cost
reviewQuestions.explain: Streaming fixes the wait, not the work. The last token still arrives when it would have.
